subject: Visualize shapes change for trajectory analysis and homogeneous of slopes test

messages.author: 0115fa6682bc8072
messages.subject: Visualize shapes change for trajectory analysis and homogeneous of slopes test
parts:
Dear all,

I am working on a dataset with a control and a mutated groups of mice, each has two growth stages. 

1. I did a trajectory analysis using the full effect mode:
fit_TA <- procD.lm(coords~groups*stages, data = gdf_size)
TA <- trajectory.analysis(fit_TA, groups = gdf_size$groups, traj.pts = gdf_size$stages, print.progress = FALSE)

The angle between trajectories has a p-value = 0.022, thus significant.

To plot the shapes represented by the trajectory terminal points, is it correct to just use the mean shapes of the groups on PC1 and PC2 of 'fit_TA$fitted', which are the fitted value of the full model?

2. I also have a similar question for visualize the size-related shape change in each group captured by homogeneity of slopes test:
fit_full <- procD.lm(coords~log(Csize)*groups, data=gdf_size, print.progress = FALSE, iter=9999)
PW2 <- pairwise(fit2, fit.null = fit1, groups = as.factor(gdf_size$groups), covariate = log(gdf_size$Csize)) 

If I don't understand it wrong, homogeneity of slopes test is based on the interaction term log(Csize)*groups. If I want to visualize the differences in size-shape relationships between groups, my idea is to first do a reduced model: 
fit_reduced ~ log(Csize) + groups, 

then isolate the interaction effect as:
reduced_effect = fit_full$fitted - fit_reduced$fitted

After that, I can then visualize the shape of the specimens using reduced_effect + mean for each specimen. I can plot the shapes associated with the smallest and largest size. Does this make sense?

Thank you very much!

Regards,
Chi

messages.author: 4d71c6e24fb21497
messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] Visualize shapes change for trajectory analysis and homogeneous of slopes test
parts:
Chi,

 

To your first question, yes. The shapes of means from fitted values can be used.

 

To your second question: maybe. If the interaction term is highly significant and with a large effect size, this means the slopes of the groups are different. In this case, one should not fit a common slope and evaluate shapes along it, as that would be the incorrect model. On the other hand, if the interaction term of size:groups is not significant, this means there is not statistical evidence of different slopes. Thus, the simpler model of size + groups may be fit (called a common slope or homogeneous slope model), and predicted values from this may be used.


Dean
